I'm reading "The Barber of Natchez'. It's a true story written by a couple of guys in the early 1900's about a successful free slave in Natchez, MS in the 1830's and '40's. It's a very informative and interesting book that was written using the subject's personal diaries (a rarity), business ledgers, and letters to friends and family. The subject, William Johnson, was born a slave in Mississippi in the 1810's and freed as a child along with his mother. It's believed that the white man that owned and freed them was Johnson's father. Long story short - William and his mom both become successful business people owning shops in downtown Natchez and the moment they have the money and the need they purchase slaves of their own. BECAUSE THAT'S WHAT PEOPLE DID BACK THEN. Another interesting note - Johnson was recommended for and received a certificate of high regard from the people of Natchez. This was given to people of color who assimilated into society and made someone of themselves. It entitled the receiver to all the same freedoms as that of a white man - excluding the rights to vote, join the military, and hold public office. Not sure what additional rights he had but it was more than that of a freed slave. The moral of the story: Johnson never worried about what other people thought - black or white. He cared about making money. And he did it - and helped make his town and family better in the process. P.S. I checked it out from my local library.
